display_name: Reading the qualifier
plain: The qualifier word in a CISM stem (FIRST, NEXT, BEST, MOST, PRIMARY) determines what kind of answer the question wants, before any content knowledge is applied.
note: PHASE 6B CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 6A/6B architecture, grounded in docs/learning/QUALIFIER-DECODER.md and docs/learning/FOUNDATION-BLUEPRINT.md. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted. Pending explicit promotion decision per docs/learning/README.md#content-status-terminology.

display_name: Authority follows accountability
plain: Decision authority in a CISM governance scenario belongs to whoever is accountable for the outcome, not to whoever has the most relevant expertise or first identified the issue.
note: PHASE 6B CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 6A/6B architecture, grounded in docs/learning/PATTERN-LIBRARY.md (P02, P03), docs/learning/ROLE-AUTHORITY-MATRIX.md, and docs/learning/DOMAIN-1-BLUEPRINT.md. Distinct from the illustrative concept.d1.policy-hierarchy / concept.d1.business-alignment entities in schema/example/ (test-only, not referenced here). Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Governance vs. management
plain: Governance sets direction, accountability, and oversight — deciding what the enterprise should achieve, how much risk it will accept, and holding the effort accountable over time. Management executes within the direction governance has already set.
note: PHASE 7B-1 CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 7A architecture and Phase 7B-1 scope, grounded in docs/learning/CONFUSING-CONCEPTS.md's existing Governance vs. Management pair and evidenced by the supplied Domain 1 source material's Information Governance Frameworks / Organizational Structures sub-areas (governance-definition questions). Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: The governance layer: Board, Steering Committee, CISO
plain: Board/Senior Management, the Security Steering Committee, and the Security Manager/CISO are three distinct governance-layer bodies performing different verbs — approve/fund/accept, prioritize/advocate/review, and develop/assess/recommend. Being involved in a decision is not the same as holding authority over it.
note: PHASE 7B-1 CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 7A architecture and Phase 7B-1 scope, grounded in docs/learning/ROLE-AUTHORITY-MATRIX.md and evidenced by the supplied Domain 1 source material's Organizational Structures, Roles, and Responsibilities sub-area (the largest single category in the source bank). Builds on concept.d1.authority-accountability rather than duplicating it — this concept is specifically about which of three governance-layer bodies performs a given verb, not the general authority-follows-accountability principle. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Data ownership and accountability
plain: The business-side data/information owner — not IT, not security, not a vendor or custodian — classifies information, defines protection requirements, and approves access, because they are accountable for that information's business value and impact.
note: PHASE 7B-1 CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 7A architecture and Phase 7B-1 scope, grounded in docs/learning/ROLE-AUTHORITY-MATRIX.md's Data Owner row and evidenced by the supplied Domain 1 source material's dense data-ownership question cluster within Organizational Structures, Roles, and Responsibilities. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Security strategy follows business direction
plain: An information security strategy exists to support the organization's actual objectives, priorities, and risk appetite — it is driven by business direction, not by which security posture is technically strongest in isolation. Strategic direction (what security needs to achieve) is distinct from implementation detail (the specific steps that follow).
note: PHASE 7B-2 CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 7A architecture and Phase 7B-2 scope (D1-U5), grounded in docs/learning/PATTERN-LIBRARY.md (P01) and evidenced by the supplied Domain 1 source material's Information Security Strategy Development sub-area (the single largest category in the source bank). Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Business justification, business case, and roadmap
plain: A security initiative is justified by connecting it to business value, risk, cost, and organizational priorities, not merely because it improves security. Strategy sets where and why security is going; a business case justifies why a specific initiative deserves support; a roadmap sequences strategic direction into practical steps over time.
note: PHASE 7B-2 CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 7A architecture and Phase 7B-2 scope (D1-U6), grounded in docs/learning/CONFUSING-CONCEPTS.md's Business Case vs. Strategy vs. Roadmap pair (approved Phase 7A, activated here) and evidenced by the supplied Domain 1 source material's Strategic Planning sub-area. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Governance effectiveness: structure and activity vs. measured outcome
plain: Frameworks and standards create structure and consistency for a security program, and GRC integrates related governance, risk, and compliance activities to reduce duplication — but none of these prove governance is effective. Effectiveness is demonstrated by measuring whether security activity produces the intended business/risk outcome, not by how much activity occurred or which framework was adopted.
note: PHASE 7B-2 CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 7A architecture and Phase 7B-2 scope (D1-U7), grounded in docs/learning/PATTERN-LIBRARY.md (P07, P14) and evidenced by the supplied Domain 1 source material's Information Governance Frameworks and Standards sub-area. Deliberately not a framework-cataloging concept — teaches why frameworks/GRC/measurement matter, not a list of named frameworks. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Legal, regulatory, and contractual requirements as risk
plain: A new legal, regulatory, or contractual requirement is a risk-management question, not an automatic trigger for immediate implementation: it must first be assessed for applicability, scope, and affected business processes before any treatment is decided, and the compliance obligation itself does not by itself pick the right role or the right action.
note: PHASE 7B-3 CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 7A architecture and Phase 7B-3 scope (D1-U8), grounded in docs/learning/PATTERN-LIBRARY.md (P02, P03), docs/learning/ROLE-AUTHORITY-MATRIX.md's Legal/Compliance row, and schema/registry/qualifiers.json's own canonical FIRST example (a new regulation's FIRST action is determining affected processes, not selecting controls) — evidenced by the supplied Domain 1 source material's Legal and Regulatory Requirements sub-area. Deliberately does not encode 'the compliance-sounding option is always correct' — see the family's invariant_reasoning. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Organizational culture and governance effectiveness
plain: Governance is not effective merely because leadership directs or publishes a policy — organizational culture (adoption, behavior, resistance to change, leadership tone and consistency) determines whether governance actually becomes real in practice. This extends pattern P07 (implementation does not prove effectiveness) to the cultural/behavioral layer: a mandate is necessary but not sufficient.
note: PHASE 7B-3 CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 7A architecture and Phase 7B-3 scope (D1-U9, Domain 1 capstone), grounded in docs/learning/PATTERN-LIBRARY.md (P07) and evidenced by the supplied Domain 1 source material's Organizational Culture sub-area. Deliberately not a general HR/change-management concept — scoped to why culture affects whether governance is effective, per the explicit Phase 7B-3 instruction. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Policy, standard, procedure, and guideline
plain: Policy states high-level, durable management direction and intent. A standard defines a mandatory boundary or requirement that links that policy to more detailed practice. A procedure defines the specific, mandatory steps taken to meet a standard or policy. A guideline offers recommended, non-mandatory practice. The distinction rests on authority, prescriptiveness, and level of detail - not a fixed document count every enterprise must maintain identically.
note: PHASE 7C CANDIDATE (Domain 1 readiness follow-up, G1) — authored by Claude Code following the Phase 7C read-only assessment's finding that this canonical docs/learning/DOMAIN-1-BLUEPRINT.md requirement ('the learner can recognize the policy/standard/procedure/guideline hierarchy') was not yet taught anywhere in Domain 1. Activates the previously-documented-but-unactivated Policy vs. Standard vs. Procedure vs. Guideline pair in docs/learning/CONFUSING-CONCEPTS.md. Taught inside lesson.d1.governance-effectiveness (U7) rather than a new unit, per explicit architect instruction. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Threat vs. vulnerability vs. risk
plain: A threat is something capable of causing harm; a vulnerability is a weakness that could be exploited; risk is what results from the combination of a threat, a vulnerability, and the business impact if the two came together - not any one of these three alone. Counting vulnerabilities, or noting that a threat exists, does not by itself tell you how much risk exists; the business consequence if exploitation actually occurred is what determines that.
note: PHASE 9B-1 CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 9A Domain 2 architecture (D2-U1). Grounded in docs/learning/PATTERN-LIBRARY.md (P12) and evidenced by the supplied Domain 2 source material's Risk Assessment and Analysis and Emerging Risk and Threat Landscape sub-areas. Deliberately scoped to Threat/Vulnerability/Risk only, per the explicit Phase 9B-1 instruction — Inherent vs. Residual Risk is deferred to a later batch where treatment/residual risk has meaning. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Risk assessment lifecycle: Context, Identify, Analyze, Evaluate
plain: Before any risk can be assessed, the objectives, scope, and criteria for the assessment must be established (Context). A specific risk is then named (Identify) before its likelihood and impact can be characterized (Analyze). Only once a risk has been analyzed can it be compared against risk appetite/tolerance criteria to judge its significance (Evaluate). Each stage depends on the one before it having actually happened - recognizing which stage a scenario describes is often the key to answering correctly.
note: PHASE 9B-1 CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 9A Domain 2 architecture (D2-U2). Grounded in docs/learning/LIFECYCLE-MODEL.md's CANONICAL Domain 2 risk lifecycle and docs/learning/PATTERN-LIBRARY.md (P04), evidenced by the supplied Domain 2 source material's Risk Assessment and Analysis sub-area. Deliberately stops at Evaluate — Treat and later stages are out of scope for this batch, per explicit instruction. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Qualitative vs. quantitative risk analysis: method fits objective
plain: Qualitative analysis uses descriptive/ordinal ratings (e.g., High/Medium/Low) and fits decisions needing a fast, relative comparison or involving impacts that don't quantify well (trust, morale, reputation). Quantitative analysis expresses risk in numeric/monetary terms and fits decisions that require a defensible dollar comparison, such as justifying a control's cost - but it requires sufficiently reliable data, and forcing numeric precision onto unreliable data is false precision, not rigor. Neither method is universally superior; the right one is the one that gives the decision enough of the right kind of information.
note: PHASE 9B-2 CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 9A Domain 2 architecture (D2-U3). Grounded in docs/learning/PATTERN-LIBRARY.md (P10 — Method Fits Objective) and evidenced by the supplied Domain 2 source material's matched-pair qualitative/quantitative fit questions (e.g., a permanent decline in customer confidence best assessed qualitatively vs. an electrical power outage best assessed quantitatively). Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Quantitative risk for decisions: AV, EF, SLE, ARO, ALE
plain: Asset Value (AV) is the value of the asset/exposure being considered. Exposure Factor (EF) is the portion of that value expected to be lost in one occurrence. Single Loss Expectancy (SLE = AV x EF) is the expected loss from one occurrence. Annualized Rate of Occurrence (ARO) is how often that occurrence is expected per year. Annualized Loss Expectancy (ALE = SLE x ARO) is the expected loss averaged over a year. ALE is one legitimate input into a treatment decision - comparing it against a control's cost is useful, but the comparison alone does not automatically decide whether to approve or reject the control; other factors (regulatory, safety, reputational, risk appetite) can still matter.
note: PHASE 9B-2 CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 9A Domain 2 architecture (D2-U4) and the CANONICAL quantitative-risk requirement in docs/learning/DOMAIN-2-BLUEPRINT.md. Grounded in docs/learning/PATTERN-LIBRARY.md (P10) and evidenced by the supplied Domain 2 source material (e.g., asset valuation as the first step in quantitative risk analysis; the ALE-limitation question). Deliberately scoped to the depth needed for a management decision, not arithmetic for its own sake, per explicit instruction. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Risk evaluation: comparing analyzed risk against criteria, appetite, and tolerance
plain: Analysis tells you what a risk looks like - its likelihood and impact. Evaluation tells you what that risk means to the organization - comparing the analyzed risk against established criteria, including risk appetite (the broad amount/type of risk the organization is willing to pursue or retain, a strategic-level posture) and risk tolerance (the acceptable variation around a specific objective or threshold, a narrower operational boundary). Evaluation determines whether an analyzed risk is acceptable as-is or requires further action - but the decision of what is actually acceptable belongs to the appropriately accountable business/risk authority, not to whoever performed the analysis.
note: PHASE 9B-3 CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 9A Domain 2 architecture (D2-U5). Grounded in docs/learning/PATTERN-LIBRARY.md (P02 - Authority Follows Accountability) and docs/learning/CONFUSING-CONCEPTS.md's approved Risk Appetite vs. Risk Tolerance pair, evidenced by the supplied Domain 2 source material's acceptable-risk-determination and appetite/tolerance-threshold questions. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Risk treatment: selecting a response that fits the business
plain: Once an evaluated risk is found unacceptable, the enterprise selects a treatment: avoid (stop the activity causing the risk), mitigate (reduce likelihood and/or impact through controls or other action), transfer/share (shift or share some financial or operational consequence with another party, such as through insurance - which does not eliminate the organization's own accountability for the risk), or accept (a knowing, authorized decision by the accountable authority to retain the risk within established criteria, not passive neglect). There is no universally strongest treatment - the best one fits the business objective, the risk level, cost, feasibility, and the organization's own risk appetite/tolerance.
note: PHASE 9B-3 CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 9A Domain 2 architecture (D2-U6). Grounded in docs/learning/PATTERN-LIBRARY.md (P01 - Business Alignment) and evidenced by the supplied Domain 2 source material's treatment-option identification questions (insurance as risk transfer, security controls as risk mitigation, stopping an activity as risk avoidance). Deliberately stops before residual-risk/validate-acceptability teaching, which belongs to D2-U7. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Residual risk and acceptability: what remains after treatment, and whether that's acceptable
plain: Inherent risk is the risk level before considering the effect of any controls or treatment; residual risk is what remains after controls/treatment have actually been applied. Applying a treatment does not mean the risk disappears - it means the risk level has changed, and that new (residual) level must itself be determined before anything else happens. Once residual risk is known, the next step is to validate whether it is acceptable relative to the enterprise's own risk appetite and tolerance - a decision for the accountable risk/business authority, not automatically for whoever selected or implemented the treatment.
note: PHASE 9B-4 CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 9A Domain 2 architecture (D2-U7). Grounded in docs/learning/CONFUSING-CONCEPTS.md's approved Inherent vs. Residual Risk pair, docs/learning/PATTERN-LIBRARY.md (P04 - No Lifecycle Jumping; P02 - Authority Follows Accountability), and evidenced by the supplied Domain 2 source material's own inherent/residual definition ('a risk prior to mitigation is called inherent risk; the risk that remains after countermeasures and controls have been implemented is residual risk') and its genuine NEXT-tagged sequencing question ('after residual risk has been determined, the enterprise should NEXT... validate that the residual risk is acceptable'). Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Risk Owner vs. Control Owner: accountability for the risk vs. accountability for a control
plain: The Risk Owner is accountable for a specific risk - they decide on treatment options, select controls, assign resources, and are accountable for managing the risk to an acceptable level. The Control Owner is accountable for a specific control's design, operation, and effectiveness - ensuring it performs as intended and reporting on its performance - but does not thereby become accountable for the underlying business risk. Operating or being technically closest to a control does not automatically grant authority over the risk it addresses; the two roles can be held by different people, and the right answer to a role question always depends on the specific verb and context in the stem, not on job title or seniority alone.
note: PHASE 9B-4 CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 9A Domain 2 architecture (D2-U8). Grounded in docs/learning/PATTERN-LIBRARY.md (P02 - Authority Follows Accountability; P03 - Role-Verb Matching) and evidenced by the supplied Domain 2 source material's own Risk Owner vs. Control Owner justifications (the risk owner is accountable for loss and approves control exceptions; the control owner ensures the control is effective but may not be accountable for loss; the risk owner's main duty is to decide on risk response/select controls/assign resources, not to personally oversee control effectiveness when a distinct control owner exists). Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Risk monitoring, reassessment, and reporting: keeping a point-in-time decision honest over time
plain: A risk decision (an acceptability judgment, a treatment choice) is made against the assumptions true at that moment - the threat environment, the business context, control effectiveness, and the risk's own likelihood and impact. None of those stay fixed. Monitoring exists to detect meaningful change in those assumptions - through indicators, thresholds, and review cadence - not to accumulate metrics for their own sake. Reassessment is the act of updating the risk judgment once monitoring reveals a material change (a major business change, new technology, a significant threat shift, a major control failure, a regulatory change, an acquisition or merger, a material incident, or a risk indicator crossing a meaningful threshold) or once a scheduled review requires it - not on every minor fluctuation, and not only after something has already gone wrong. Reporting closes the loop: it delivers the right information, at the right level of detail, to the audience that actually needs to act on it. A board or senior management generally needs decision-relevant risk information (for example, that a specific risk now exceeds tolerance and requires a decision), not raw technical telemetry or a count of completed activities - 'we performed 50 assessments' is activity; 'three risks moved beyond tolerance and need an executive decision' is decision-useful.
note: PHASE 9B-5 CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 9A Domain 2 architecture (D2-U9). Grounded in docs/learning/PATTERN-LIBRARY.md (P11 - Audience-Appropriate Communication; P15 - Closing the Loop; P07 - Implementation ≠ Effectiveness, recalled from Domain 1) and evidenced by the supplied Domain 2 source material's own monitoring/reassessment/reporting content: lag indicators as what BEST helps report changes in risk levels tied to control compliance; effectiveness of managing business risk BEST measured by incidents causing significant financial loss or business disruption, not by counts of assessments performed, vulnerabilities identified, or unmitigated findings; key risk indicators reported to senior management (tied to critical business assets) as MOST appropriate for ongoing, timely decisions, versus risk-assessment results, historical loss data, or scenario-analysis results; business objectives as the MOST important element when planning what to report to senior management; a vendor acquisition (an enterprise acquiring the enterprise's key software vendor) as the PRIMARY candidate for risk reassessment, versus routine, already-effective control alerts. Not a reproduction or paraphrase of any specific source question. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Embedding risk management into the business, and the Domain 2 synthesis
plain: Risk management that lives only inside the security function, separate from how the business actually makes decisions, gets bypassed by those decisions - a procurement decision made without risk input, a disagreement between a business manager and the security manager resolved by whichever one is more persistent rather than by executive judgment, a new initiative launched without anyone asking what stage of risk management it actually needs. Embedding risk management into the business means risk reasoning is present at the point normal business decisions are made - procurement, new initiatives, technology acquisition, process change - not bolted on afterward as a separate compliance step, and that genuine disagreements between a business owner and a risk/security function are escalated to the accountable executive authority for a decision, not resolved by either party unilaterally. This is also where Domain 2's individual pieces - fundamentals, the assessment lifecycle, method selection, evaluation, treatment, residual risk and acceptability, ownership, and monitoring/reassessment/reporting - connect into one continuous chain that a business scenario actually walks through, rather than remaining separate lessons about separate stages.
note: PHASE 9B-5 CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per approved Phase 9A Domain 2 architecture (D2-U10) and the Phase 9B-4 founder-approved Domain Synthesis / Capstone principle (docs/learning/CURRICULUM-BLUEPRINT.md, docs/learning/DOMAIN-2-BLUEPRINT.md's D2-U10 section). Grounded in docs/learning/PATTERN-LIBRARY.md (P09 - Security Embedded in Business Process; P08 - Risk-Driven Prioritization) and evidenced by the supplied Domain 2 source material's own business-embedding content: appropriate procurement processes as the FIRST step to manage risk from a new critical IT-system acquisition (identifying risk within the procurement process itself, not merely obtaining budget approval or requiring risk acceptance after the fact); a disagreement between the information security manager and a business department manager over a completed risk assessment/BIA resolved BEST by reviewing the result with executive management, not by either party's unilateral decision. This concept intentionally reinforces D2-U6 (treatment/prioritization) and D2-U8 (ownership) reasoning in a live business-process setting rather than teaching new vocabulary, and serves as the connective concept for the Domain 2 synthesis/capstone experience - it does not introduce any Domain 2 concept beyond what D2-U1 through D2-U9 already teach. Not a reproduction or paraphrase of any specific source question. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Security program vs. strategy vs. technical implementation
plain: An information security program is the coordinated management structure — people, process, technology, and resources organized around priority — that turns approved information security strategy and business objectives into organized execution. It is not the strategy itself (which sets direction and desired outcomes), and it is not any single technical control, tool, or project (which is one piece of coordinated execution). A collection of security technologies, however capable, is not a program unless it is organized around what the approved strategy actually requires; program resources and priorities should trace back to that requirement, not exist independently of it.
note: DOMAIN 3 CURRICULUM ARCHITECTURE APPROVED / D3-U1 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-3-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md and the Architect's D3-U1/U2 authoring directive. Grounded in the supplied Domain 3 source material's 3A1 (Information Security Program Resources) sub-area — specifically its genuinely program/strategy-level questions (program development beginning from management's desired outcomes; the BEST business-value justification for program investment; the BEST response to reduced program funding), not its many mistagged deeply-technical questions (PKI, biometrics, WLAN, etc.), which were reviewed and deliberately excluded as off-topic for this concept per the explicit instruction not to reduce U1 to resource budgeting or technical architecture. Deliberately teaches NO canonical Domain 3 lifecycle (none exists — see docs/learning/LIFECYCLE-MODEL.md's explicit withdrawal of the earlier Domain 1/3 staged-lifecycle draft); the strategy/program/controls relationship is taught as a conceptual sequencing aid only. Meridian Manufacturing acquisition context is the approved recurring reference story, kept business-centered per explicit instruction (no OT/ICS technical content). Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Asset identification, classification, and ownership accountability
plain: A security program cannot decide what deserves protection, or how much, until the organization knows what information and assets it actually has (identification) and how important each one is to the business (classification, based on criticality and sensitivity — not acquisition cost, threat exposure, or ease of protection). Classification is what turns an inventory into something the program can act on: it drives the specific handling and protection requirements an asset receives, and an incomplete or outdated inventory undermines the program's ability to prioritize its activities at all. Newly acquired or newly discovered assets — for example, systems and records brought in through a business acquisition — are not exempt: they must be identified and classified into the enterprise's program the same way any other asset is. Accountability for setting that classification belongs to the business owner of the information or asset, not to whoever technically maintains it — the same accountable-owner distinction the enterprise already applies to data generally.
note: DOMAIN 3 CURRICULUM ARCHITECTURE APPROVED / D3-U2 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-3-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md and the Architect's D3-U1/U2 authoring directive. Grounded in the supplied Domain 3 source material's 3A2 (Information Asset Identification and Classification) sub-area (classification based on criticality/sensitivity, not cost; the information owner — not the custodian — determines classification; an incomplete asset catalog is the GREATEST challenge to risk-prioritization). Deliberately scoped as its OWN Domain 3 concept (concept.d3.asset-classification), distinct from the existing concept.d1.data-ownership — see the BUG-001 cross-domain identity safety note in DOMAIN-3-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md §9 — recalling that Domain 1 concept via the lesson's own prerequisite/recall chain rather than re-teaching or sharing its identity. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Mandatory vs. discretionary program artifacts
plain: Within a security program, policies, standards, and procedures are binding - they establish requirements the organization must follow - while guidelines are discretionary, offering recommended practice that business management may adapt within its own areas of control. The program-governance question is not how formal, detailed, or official an artifact sounds, but what it actually commits the organization to: does its own language create an obligation, or does it merely recommend? A procedure's binding, step-by-step nature is also why it is worth formally documenting - without that documentation, its execution cannot be consistent and repeatable across whoever carries it out.
note: DOMAIN 3 U3/U4 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-3-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md and the Architect's D3-U3/U4 authoring directive. Grounded in the supplied Domain 3 source material's 3A4 (Information Security Policies, Procedures, and Guidelines) sub-area: a statement using mandatory ('must') language belongs in a policy regardless of its title or formatting; guidelines are recommendations business management may adapt within its own areas of control, while policies/standards/procedures cannot be discretionary; procedures are formally documented primarily so execution is repeatable and consistent, not primarily to satisfy an audit or build metrics. This is deliberately NOT a re-teach of Domain 1's existing concept.d1.policy-artifact-hierarchy (policy/standard/procedure/guideline definitions, already taught in lesson.d1.governance-effectiveness) - that concept is recalled through this lesson's own prerequisite chain (D3-U3 -> D3-U1 -> ... -> D1-U7), never re-taught or reused as this concept's own id, per the BUG-001 cross-domain identity safety note in DOMAIN-3-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md §9. The new Domain 3 angle is reasoning from an artifact's actual governance effect (binding vs. discretionary) rather than its title, tone, or formality. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Control design and selection by purpose
plain: A security control's classification - preventive, detective, corrective, or compensating - follows what the control is actually intended to accomplish in the specific scenario, not its technology name, vendor category, or how sophisticated it sounds. Preventive controls stop an event from occurring; detective controls identify that one has occurred; corrective controls reduce or recover from its impact after it has occurred; compensating controls provide an alternative safeguard when a control a policy or standard actually requires cannot be applied, chosen only after assessing the resulting risk. Selecting or designing a control is itself a risk-driven decision: its objectives should trace to the actual risk being addressed and the enterprise's risk appetite, not to what is newest, most expensive, most familiar, or easiest to deploy.
note: DOMAIN 3 U3/U4 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-3-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md and the Architect's D3-U3/U4 authoring directive. Grounded in the supplied Domain 3 source material's 3B1 (Information Security Control Design and Selection) sub-area, the largest Knowledge Statement area in Domain 3: a corrective control's purpose is to reduce/recover from impact, not to prevent or detect; preventive-control objectives should be developed PRIMARILY from risk aligned with the enterprise's risk appetite, not industry-standard checklists, monitoring-tool threat levels, or SLA uptime targets; when a required control cannot be applied, the security manager should first assess risk and identify a compensating control, not skip the requirement or halt progress. The 'risk aligned with risk appetite, not compliance-checklist volume' finding directly recalls Domain 2's risk-driven-prioritization pattern (P08) as reinforcement, not new content. Builds on concept.d3.asset-classification (D3-U2) and concept.d3.policy-governance (D3-U3): what is being protected and what is mandatorily required both motivate the scenario. Per the approved architecture's explicit caution, this does not manufacture a vocabulary-heavy lesson around the literal title 'Control Owner' (absent from the Domain 3 source corpus) - the primary target is control purpose and risk-driven selection, not role-title memorization. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Control implementation vs. genuine integration
plain: A control can be implemented - deployed, documented, installed - without being meaningfully integrated into the actual business process it is supposed to protect. Implementation is a technical or administrative state; integration means the control actually operates inside real day-to-day workflow, embedded in how work already gets done, rather than running as a separate, parallel, security-only or compliance-only activity alongside it. A control that lives outside the business process it protects is easy for that process to bypass or ignore, regardless of how completely it was implemented.
note: DOMAIN 3 U5/U6 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-3-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md and the Architect's D3-U5/U6 authoring directive. Grounded in the supplied Domain 3 source material's 3B2 (Information Security Control Implementation and Integrations) sub-area: a process owner - not a system analyst, quality control manager, or the security manager alone - implements and maintains the security level for a specific business application, because the process owner has the most knowledge of that application's actual needs; integrating multiple activities is best achieved through a coordinating structure (architecture), not ad hoc parallel effort. Source-grounding gap, reported transparently: the large majority of 3B2-tagged questions in the raw source are deeply technical (email-transport encryption, firewall/DMZ placement, log-storage architecture) rather than genuinely about implementation-vs-integration reasoning at a management level; these were reviewed and deliberately excluded, mirroring the same mistagging pattern already documented for 3A1 in D3-U1's own authoring note. The primary reasoning target instead reuses the existing CANONICAL Pattern P09 (Security Embedded in Business Process, already explicitly flagged as applying most directly to Domain 3 operational-process embedding), including its own approved change-management and HR-onboarding/offboarding example scenarios, rather than inventing new reasoning. Builds on concept.d3.control-design-selection (D3-U4) - the control chosen there is what now needs to become genuinely integrated. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Existence and implementation vs. demonstrated effectiveness
plain: Evidence that a control exists, was deployed, or was completed as an activity proves implementation - not effectiveness. A tool being installed, a policy existing, staff completing a required activity, or a procedure being documented are all facts about activity, not proof the control is actually achieving the outcome it was selected for. Effectiveness requires evidence of that specific outcome, matched to the control's own purpose - and once a control is genuinely tested and evaluated, any gap it reveals becomes the residual risk the enterprise must still decide whether to accept.
note: DOMAIN 3 U5/U6 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-3-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md and the Architect's D3-U5/U6 authoring directive. Grounded in the supplied Domain 3 source material's 3B3 (Information Security Control Testing and Evaluation) sub-area: risk controls are sufficient only when residual risk is at or below the enterprise's risk acceptance level, not simply because controls exist; achieving the control's own objective is the most important benefit to consider when reviewing risk-treatment options, ahead of cost savings or regulatory alignment alone; a virus-detection tool's effectiveness depends on current definition files, not on whether the software is merely installed and running. This is Domain 3's single most load-bearing reasoning pattern per docs/learning/DOMAIN-3-BLUEPRINT.md, and reuses the existing CANONICAL Pattern P07 (Implementation ≠ Effectiveness, already explicitly flagged as applying most directly to Domain 3 control effectiveness) rather than inventing new reasoning - this is that pattern finally receiving its own dedicated Domain 3 unit, not a new pattern. The 'residual risk ≤ acceptance level' finding is a direct, source-evidenced recall of Domain 2's existing concept.d2.residual-risk-acceptability (D2-U7), reachable through this lesson's own cumulative prerequisite chain - reinforcement, not new Domain 2 content. Builds on concept.d3.control-implementation-integration (D3-U5) - the control now genuinely integrated into operations is what testing/evaluation must verify actually works. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Security awareness & training: activity vs. behavior change
plain: Awareness and training are related but not the same activity. Awareness is the ongoing, broad effort to keep every employee conscious of expected security behavior and the consequences of compliance and noncompliance in their own job. Training goes further: it builds role-specific skill and judgment for the people whose job responsibilities create a specific risk exposure, and is most effective when its content and delivery are customized to that audience rather than delivered as one generic module for everyone. Delivering either one - sending the module, collecting a signature, recording a completion percentage - is an activity. The program's actual purpose is changing the behavior that produces risk, and threats keep changing, so that behavior change has to be renewed rather than achieved once. The evidence that the program is working is a change in behavior (for example, more suspicious messages being reported) or a measurable reduction in the risk it targets - never the completion count or the acknowledgment signature by itself. Because people are frequently the point where a technical control can be bypassed, technical measures alone do not remove the need for this people-and-process work.
note: DOMAIN 3 U7/U8 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-3-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md and the Architect's D3-U7/U8 authoring directive. Grounded in the supplied Domain 3 source material's 3B4 (Information Security Awareness and Training) sub-area: the BEST metric for training effectiveness is an increase in reported incidents (staff paying more attention), not a completion rate, password-reset count, or access-violation count; the PRIMARY objective of awareness is to influence employee behavior, not merely to ensure policy is read/understood; role-specific/customized training is consistently the MOST effective delivery method, more effective than a single general module for all staff; awareness/training must be renewed because threats and vulnerabilities change constantly; end-user awareness is repeatedly identified as the BEST defense against phishing/social-engineering, ahead of purely technical controls (filters, IDS, encryption); active awareness programs PRIMARILY influence residual risk (an administrative control reducing vulnerability), a direct, source-evidenced tie to Domain 2's existing concept.d2.residual-risk-acceptability and to D3-U6's own effectiveness reasoning (P07), reused here for a different reasoning target (training delivery vs. behavior change) rather than repeated verbatim. Source-grounding note: unlike 3B2/3B3, this sub-area's raw source material is already almost entirely management-level (no mistagged deep-technical items requiring exclusion); one item (a live social-engineering phone-verification callback procedure) was excluded as incident-response/verification procedure rather than awareness-program design or evaluation, and is out of scope for this unit rather than silently folded in. Builds on concept.d3.control-testing-evaluation (D3-U6): the same implementation-vs-effectiveness reasoning is now applied to people/process measures rather than technical or procedural controls. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: External services: performance can move outside the enterprise; accountability does not
plain: When an enterprise engages a vendor, outsourcer, or service/cloud provider to perform a function, responsibility for actually carrying out that work can move outside the organization - but accountability for the resulting business outcome, and for the risk it creates, remains with the enterprise and its accountable business owner. Security requirements should be established and communicated to the provider from the beginning of the relationship, when the business is defining what it actually needs, not added after a contract is already signed. A contract or service level agreement can require a security posture, but the contract's existence is not itself the assurance that the requirement is being met - ongoing, independent verification (most effectively periodic audits/reviews of the provider's actual practice) is what confirms that. A provider's own claim or third-party certification is useful context, but it does not substitute for the enterprise's own assurance activity. When a long-standing provider's performance disappoints, the first question is usually whether the agreement itself still reflects the enterprise's current business requirements, not simply whether the provider is meeting the old ones.
note: DOMAIN 3 U7/U8 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-3-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md and the Architect's D3-U7/U8 authoring directive. Grounded in the supplied Domain 3 source material's 3B5 (Management of External Services) sub-area: ownership/responsibility for the adequate protection of data stored at a third party remains with the outsourcing enterprise; information security should be involved from when requirements are being established, not at contract negotiation or later; a periodic, independent audit/review is repeatedly identified as the MOST effective way to ensure a provider's compliance, ahead of contracts, SLAs, penetration testing, or the provider's own claims/certifications; once a vendor contract for a service is signed, the security manager's NEXT step is establishing ongoing vendor monitoring (a genuine source-supported sequencing item, not a manufactured lifecycle); when a long-standing vendor disappoints senior management, the FIRST step is confirming the agreement itself still reflects current business requirements, before assessing vendor capability or automating reporting. Reuses the existing CANONICAL Pattern P02 (Authority Follows Accountability, already established in Domain 1 via concept.d1.authority-accountability and reused in D3-U2's concept.d3.asset-classification) rather than inventing a new pattern - the Domain 3 application is that accountability for a business outcome does not move even when performance of the underlying work does. Builds on concept.d3.awareness-training-effectiveness (D3-U7): both units conclude that an activity (training delivered; a contract signed) is not itself the evidence the enterprise needs. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Program metrics and reporting: the right measure, for the right audience
plain: A metric is only useful if it connects to what the program is actually trying to achieve and to the decision its recipient needs to make - measuring something merely because it is easy to count does not make it useful. Activity and output metrics (how many controls exist, what percentage of staff completed training, how many patches were applied) describe what happened, not whether the program is producing its intended result; a metric tied to the program's own objectives, reported as a trend over time rather than an isolated number, is what actually shows whether the program is working and improving. Different audiences need different information: senior management and the board generally need decision-relevant business/risk information - the state and direction of risk exposure, what changed, what needs a decision - not the raw operational detail an operational team would instead need to act on the same underlying facts. Four commonly required measurement types answer different questions rather than being interchangeable names for the same thing: a key performance indicator (KPI) measures how well a process is performing against its own goal; a key risk indicator (KRI) signals rising risk exposure before it becomes a loss event; a key control indicator (KCI) measures whether a specific control is operating as designed; an objective and key result (OKR) frames a goal and the measurable results that would show progress toward it, generally at a more strategic/planning level than the other three.
note: DOMAIN 3 U9/U10 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-3-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md and the Architect's D3-U9/U10 authoring directive. Grounded in the supplied Domain 3 source material's 3A5 (Information Security Program Metrics) and 3B6 (Information Security Program Communications and Reporting) sub-areas, combined per the approved architecture as two halves of one reasoning arc: metrics should be developed from security objectives, not residual risk/incident statistics alone; trends in incident frequency (not isolated counts) carry strategic value, while raw operational figures (privileged-access counts, downtime, vulnerability-scan results) are operational; the single most significant attribute of a good metric is that it is meaningful/relevant to its recipient; a quarterly executive report is best served by an overall trend, not a percentage or raw count; the percentage of control objectives accomplished (tied to the program's own objectives) is one of the best metrics for evaluating program results, ahead of controls-implemented counts or policy-compliance percentages; a specific operational metric (email virus-quarantine effectiveness) is most useful to the information security manager who can act on it, not the board; the primary reason for using metrics is to enable continuous, steady improvement. A single, directly on-point source item explicitly distinguishes all four required measurement types together: KCIs 'provide feedback on control performance only,' KRIs 'help provide early warnings about materializing risk... but not the overall security profile,' OKRs are 'useful in setting goals... but would not provide insight into performance itself,' and KPIs 'provide a comparison between expected and achieved performance and best provide feedback... on the overall effectiveness of the information security program' — this is the item this unit's KPI-vs-KRI-vs-KCI-vs-OKR reasoning is built on. Source-grounding gap, reported transparently per the approved architecture's own §3 gap note: KPI/KRI/KCI/OKR are a CANONICAL, blueprint-mandated requirement (see docs/learning/DOMAIN-3-BLUEPRINT.md and docs/learning/CONFUSING-CONCEPTS.md's own [CANDIDATE] KPI-vs-KRI-vs-KCI-vs-OKR entry, whose phrasing this concept follows) that is thin in raw question-bank frequency, not a source-frequency-heavy area - taught here as concise, decision-relevant distinctions rather than a vocabulary drill. Reuses two existing CANONICAL patterns rather than inventing new ones: P07 (Implementation ≠ Effectiveness, Domain 3's own load-bearing pattern since D3-U6, reapplied here to metric selection - an activity/output count is not evidence of program effectiveness) and P11 (Audience-Appropriate Communication, established in Domain 2's concept.d2.risk-monitoring-reporting and reused here for its first Domain 3 application). Builds on concept.d3.external-services-accountability (D3-U8): the vendor relationships and control work established across D3-U1 through D3-U8 are what this unit's metrics and reports must now actually measure and communicate. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: The security program as one connected management capability
plain: An information security program is not a policy document, a control catalog, a technology stack, a training course, a vendor contract, or a metrics dashboard - each of those is one artifact the program produces or uses along the way. The program itself is the coordinated management capability that translates approved business direction into sustained, measured, business-aligned security outcomes: it decides what to protect and why, establishes what is mandatorily required, selects and integrates the controls that protect what was classified, verifies those controls actually work, extends the same expectations to people and to external providers, and measures and reports whether the whole effort is achieving its objective - then feeds what it learns back into the next cycle. A real management situation rarely arrives labeled with which one of these pieces it belongs to; recognizing which piece is actually in play - is this a classification question, an accountability question, an effectiveness question, a reporting question, or some combination - matters more than knowing any single piece in isolation.
note: DOMAIN 3 U9/U10 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE (D3-U10, Program Synthesis / Capstone) — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-3-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md §10 (Synthesis / capstone design) and the Architect's D3-U9/U10 authoring directive, and per the general Domain Synthesis/Capstone principle in docs/learning/CURRICULUM-BLUEPRINT.md, mirroring the precedent set by Domain 2's own D2-U10 (concept.d2.risk-management-embedding-synthesis). This concept intentionally introduces no new Domain 3 fact beyond what D3-U1 through D3-U9 already teach; it is the connective concept for integrated-practice questions that each combine two or more previously taught D3-U1-U9 reasoning targets in one live business scenario, per docs/learning/LIFECYCLE-MODEL.md's approved, non-canonical Domain 3 conceptual relationship ('strategy -> program -> controls -> measurement/improvement') - never a manufactured stage-by-stage lifecycle, never tested as a stage-location question. related_patterns lists only the patterns actually exercised by this batch's capstone variants (P07, P02, P11); each variant's own `patterns` field tags only that variant's own most-salient pattern, exactly mirroring the precedent set by family.d2.risk-management-synthesis. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Incident management begins before the incident: readiness, roles, and authority
plain: An incident response plan's purpose is to control the impact of a disruptive event within acceptable levels and preserve business resiliency - it does not exist to prevent incidents from happening in the first place, and it is not the same plan as business continuity (which keeps critical operations running) or disaster recovery (which restores specific interrupted technology). Readiness means the organization has already decided - before any incident occurs - who has authority to make key decisions (such as declaring an incident or notifying affected parties), what roles and responsibilities each person carries, and how incidents will be categorized by severity so that response time, reporting, and staffing can all be calibrated to that categorization. A written plan is a necessary starting point, not proof of readiness by itself: readiness is demonstrated by how quickly the organization can actually move from detecting a potential incident to initiating a response, and by whether the plan has been genuinely tested - not merely drafted and filed away.
note: DOMAIN 4 U1/U2 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE (D4-U1, Program Foundations & Readiness) — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md and the Architect's D4-U1/U2 authoring directive. This is Domain 4's entry point, the first production batch authored for this domain. Grounded in the supplied Domain 4 source material's 4A1 (Incident Response Plan) sub-area: gaining senior leadership's buy-in is directly identified as the most significant challenge, and the necessary first step, in developing an incident management plan; the first step in developing an incident response plan specifically is establishing a categorization scheme (by likelihood/impact), since response-time targets, reporting thresholds, and staffing needs all derive from it; responsibility for notifying external parties of a breach should be determined during plan development, not after detection or after senior management 'approves' an incident (a role the source explicitly states senior management does not perform - incident response teams confirm incidents); the primary business objective of incident management is controlling impact within acceptable levels, and the most important purpose of an incident response plan specifically is promoting business resiliency - explicitly distinguished in-source from preventing incidents (which it cannot guarantee) and from ensuring business continuity (a separate plan's job); defined roles and responsibilities (not policies/procedures knowledge, forensic skill, or reporting-line structure) contribute most to incident response team efficiency; the best indicator of incident response team readiness is the time between detection and response initiation, not detection time or total resolution time alone - readiness is demonstrated by response speed, not by a plan's mere existence; a formal, repeatable, tested methodology matters because its evidence of due diligence supports legal/liability claims. Reuses two existing CANONICAL patterns already approved for Domain 4 (see schema/registry/patterns.json's applicable_domains): P06 (Purpose vs. Activity - the plan's true purpose is impact control/resiliency, not the procedural steps like containment/eradication, which are activities in service of that purpose, nor incident prevention or ticket-closing) and P02 (Authority Follows Accountability - who has authority for key decisions is established during plan development, not improvised during an active incident). No new pattern invented. Prerequisite is lesson.d3.program-synthesis (Domain 3's own capstone) only, continuing the same full, cumulative cross-domain recall chain every prior domain's own first unit has used (D3-U1 itself prerequisited on Domain 2's own capstone). Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Business impact analysis: prioritizing recovery by business impact, not technical importance
plain: A business impact analysis (BIA) determines which business functions and supporting systems matter most by assessing the impact their disruption would create - not their technical sophistication, how recently they were deployed, their replacement cost, or the threats/vulnerabilities that might affect them (that is the separate work of a risk assessment). The people best positioned to provide this input are the business units and process owners who actually depend on each function, not IT or security staff alone. A BIA's core outputs - which functions are critical, how quickly each must be restored (recovery time objective, RTO), and how much data loss each can tolerate (recovery point objective, RPO) - are what business continuity planning is then built on: the BIA is performed first and feeds the business continuity plan, not the other way around. Because the cost of a disruption typically grows the longer it continues, and because what counts as critical can change as the business changes, a BIA is revisited periodically and after material change, not performed once and filed away. Incident response, business continuity, and disaster recovery are three different plans answering three different questions: incident response manages the security incident itself and aims to keep its impact within acceptable levels; business continuity plans keep critical business operations functioning if the incident's impact grows large enough to threaten them; disaster recovery restores the specific technology or services that were interrupted. Business continuity and disaster recovery are invoked only if an incident's impact escalates far enough to require them - not automatically, for every incident that incident response itself is able to resolve.
note: DOMAIN 4 U1/U2 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE (D4-U2, Business Impact Analysis & Prioritization) — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md and the Architect's D4-U1/U2 authoring directive. Grounded in the supplied Domain 4 source material's 4A2 (Business Impact Analysis) sub-area: a BIA is the best tool for determining priority of restoration (not total cost of ownership, annual loss expectancy, or residual risk); the primary BIA stakeholders are representatives from various business units/departments (not IT personnel alone, not senior management alone, not risk/audit alone); essential BIA ingredients are downtime tolerance, resources, and criticality (explicitly NOT cost-as-percentage-of-budget, BC testing methodology, or crisis-team structure, which belong to business continuity planning, not the BIA itself); BIA actions include listing critical business resources and identifying disruption impacts/allowable outage times (explicitly NOT identifying threats/vulnerabilities, which is risk assessment, and NOT developing notification/activation procedures, which is business continuity planning); a system's value in a BIA is based on the opportunity cost of losing the function, not the cost to recover or recreate it; a new application does not automatically deserve top recovery priority merely because it is new; the BIA process is performed first and its results (critical functions, dependencies, resources, recovery requirements) are the essential inputs business continuity planning is then built on - directly source-confirmed, not inferred. IR-vs-BCP-vs-DRP distinction explicitly source-confirmed per this batch's required validation (see docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-U1-U2-GATE-RECORD.md): a business continuity plan 'would be triggered during the execution of the incident response plan in case it developed into a disaster causing serious business interruption' (source, verbatim), and the most important purpose of an incident response plan is explicitly distinguished in-source from 'ensuring business continuity,' which is a separate plan's job. RTO and RPO are used with the exact definitions already established in docs/learning/CONFUSING-CONCEPTS.md's existing RTO-vs-RPO-vs-SDO-vs-MTO entry (not redefined here); MTO/AIW/SDO are deliberately not taught in depth in this unit, reserved for D4-U8's own dedicated BCP/DRP-boundary treatment, per the binding instruction not to turn this unit into a continuity-certification course. Reuses the existing CANONICAL Pattern P01 (Business Alignment, already approved for Domain 4) - recovery priority reflects business impact/value, not a technical characteristic of the system itself - rather than inventing a new pattern. Builds on concept.d4.incident-management-readiness (D4-U1): the readiness/authority decisions D4-U1 establishes are what this unit's impact analysis now informs and prioritizes. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Incident classification and severity: confirm and categorize before acting
plain: Not every event is an incident, and not every incident carries the same business impact or urgency. Before choosing a response, the organization must first confirm what has actually happened - an unconfirmed event is not yet an incident - and then classify it against a predefined categorization scheme so that response resources, authority, and escalation are applied consistently rather than improvised in the moment. Severity should be assessed by business impact - financial, legal/regulatory, operational, and reputational consequences, and the specific assets/processes affected - rather than by how technically dramatic or complex an event appears: a highly sophisticated attempt against a low-value system can be less severe than a simple compromise that exposes sensitive data. The primary reason to classify and categorize incidents is to use limited response resources where they matter most, and an effective classification scheme is tailored to the organization's own business context, built with input from the people who understand that context - not adopted wholesale from generic industry categories, nor assigned to the technical response team alone.
note: DOMAIN 4 U3/U4 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE (D4-U3, Incident Classification / Severity) — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md and the Architect's D4-U3/U4 authoring directive. Grounded in the supplied Domain 4 source material's 4A5 (Incident Classification/Categorization) sub-area, read comprehensively: an incident is classified by the nature and intent of the actual act (e.g. an intentional, privileged-access misuse by an insider is classified as 'insider threat,' not 'configuration error,' 'privilege escalation,' or 'denial of service,' each of which fits a different actual fact pattern); the PRIMARY purpose of classification/categorization, and of triage, is using limited incident resources more efficiently, not preventing recurrence, ensuring containment, or improving team awareness; during the detection-and-analysis phase, a category is assigned based on financial/legal/regulatory/operational/reputational impact - media management and root-cause accountability belong to later phases; a data breach (sensitive data accessed/disclosed/used by unauthorized parties) is a more precise, and therefore better, classification than a broader label like 'unauthorized access' or 'security incident' when the facts support it; the BEST factor for escalating to an internal response team is the incident's classification/categorization level itself, because that level defines likely impact and urgency - not technical complexity/duration alone, not affected-assets/processes alone (useful for notifying business stakeholders, not for responder escalation), not responder experience alone; the MOST effective way to ensure proper classification is a framework tailored to the organization's own business context, built with stakeholder input - not generic industry-standard categories alone, not assigned to the incident response team alone, and not outsourced to a third party. Reuses two existing CANONICAL patterns already approved for Domain 4 (schema/registry/patterns.json's applicable_domains): P04 (No Lifecycle Jumping - the domain's central governing-pattern family, its first true Domain 4 use: acting on an unconfirmed event as if it were already a classified incident, or escalating before classification, is jumping ahead of the Identify/Confirm work) and P01 (Business Alignment - severity follows business impact, not technical drama). No new pattern invented. Builds on concept.d4.business-impact-analysis-prioritization (D4-U2): the same impact-based reasoning BIA establishes for recovery priority is now applied to incident severity. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Escalation and communication: the right information, to the right audience, through the right authority
plain: Once an incident is classified, the organization still has to get the right information to the right people, through an authorized path, at the right time - escalation and communication are themselves management disciplines, not an instinct to notify everyone immediately or an impulse to say nothing at all. Escalation guidelines should be built from risk and impact analysis - the same business-impact reasoning that drives classification - so that urgent, high-impact incidents reach the people with the authority to act on them faster than routine ones; insufficiently defined escalation paths are one of the greatest obstacles to effective incident management generally. Different audiences need different information: senior management and executives need the business impact and corrective actions being taken, not a raw technical log; the media should hear only specifically prepared, pre-authorized messages from one identified spokesperson, never an unplanned comment from whoever happens to be asked. Deciding whether and how to notify external parties - regulators, affected customers, the press - is a business decision that belongs to management, following the organization's own communication plan, not a call the information security manager, the incident response team, or an involved third-party provider makes unilaterally; a third party performing work related to the incident does not inherit the organization's own accountability for that decision. Communication exists to keep relevant parties informed so they can take the right action - not to generate reassurance, and not to generate noise.
note: DOMAIN 4 U3/U4 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE (D4-U4, Escalation & Communications) — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md and the Architect's D4-U3/U4 authoring directive. Grounded in the supplied Domain 4 source material's 4B4 (Incident Response Communications) sub-area, read comprehensively: the most important item to report to the CIO/senior management after a significant breach is the impact and corrective actions taken, not a technical log summary, a comparative industry analysis, or a business case for new controls (each explicitly rejected in-source as 'too technical' or premature); the primary purpose of a crisis communication plan is providing procedures for who/how to contact stakeholders, not minimizing information loss (incident response's job) or covering only media contact (one part of a larger plan); on discovering exposed confidential data, the FIRST step is notifying the data owner before any unilateral technical action; the greatest challenge to effective incident management is insufficiently defined escalation paths; when a breach affecting customer data is confirmed, data owners are notified FIRST - the steering committee, customers, and regulators are notified later per policy/regulatory requirements, not simultaneously; the MOST important consideration for media interaction is a specifically drafted message from one authorized spokesperson, not refusing all comment, not referring media to authorities, and not reporting losses/strategy directly; the BEST input for defining escalation guidelines is a risk and impact analysis - directly connecting this unit back to D4-U2's BIA reasoning; communication regarding security events with legal implications is explicitly a business decision belonging to management, not the information security manager contacting external authorities directly; effective incident management in a large enterprise is MOST dependent on effective communication/reporting processes, and the factor most likely to result in incident identification in the first place is security awareness training (a direct, source-evidenced Domain 3 (D3-U7) callback) - communication's own best reason for being maintained is ensuring all relevant parties are informed and can take appropriate action, not guaranteeing understanding, preventing breaches, or saving cost. PATTERN REGISTRY NOTE: this unit's core reasoning (audience-appropriate reporting to the CIO/senior management, technical-detail-inappropriate-for-executives) is a direct, strong match for the existing CANONICAL Pattern P11 (Audience-Appropriate Communication) - already established in Domain 2 (concept.d2.risk-monitoring-reporting) and Domain 3 (concept.d3.program-metrics-reporting), and explicitly named as this unit's expected Domain 3 cross-domain reinforcement target in the Architect's own D4-U3/U4 authoring directive. P11's applicable_domains in schema/registry/patterns.json did not yet include domain.d4 (only d1/d2/d3); a single, narrow metadata addition (domain.d4 added to that existing array) was made to reflect this authorized, source-grounded usage - the pattern's own meaning/recognition_clues/nuance/memory_rule were not altered. Also reuses P02 (Authority Follows Accountability, already Domain-4-approved) for the external/legal-communication-authority and third-party-accountability reasoning. No new pattern invented. Builds on concept.d4.incident-classification-severity (D4-U3): the same classification/severity judgment now determines who is told what, and how urgently. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Incident containment: limiting harm without mistaking it for resolution
plain: Once an incident has been confirmed, classified, and escalated through the right authority path, containment is the next priority: limiting further harm and stopping the incident from spreading while preserving the organization's ability to manage it properly. Containment is not the same as eradication (removing the root cause), recovery (restoring normal operations), or declaring the incident resolved - a contained incident is still an active incident, not a finished one. The right containment scope follows the incident's actual severity and business impact rather than the instinct to shut down as much as possible: isolating the specific affected system or network segment is usually more appropriate than a broad, indiscriminate shutdown that disrupts parts of the business that were never at risk, without a corresponding security benefit. Because a hasty containment action - rebooting a system, restoring it from backup, or otherwise changing its state - can destroy the evidence needed to understand what happened, effective containment decisions weigh evidence and investigation needs alongside the urgency to limit damage, rather than treating speed as the only consideration.
note: DOMAIN 4 U5/U6 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE (D4-U5, Containment) — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md and the Architect's D4-U5/U6 authoring directive. Grounded in the supplied Domain 4 source material's 4B3 (Incident Containment Methods) sub-area, read comprehensively (17 questions): containment is the FIRST priority once an incident is confirmed - ahead of documentation, damage assessment, root-cause analysis, or notifying law enforcement (root-cause analysis/removal is explicitly identified as part of eradication, a separate, later process); containment scope should match the incident's actual impact rather than defaulting to the broadest possible action - isolating the affected network segment (not shutting off all network access points, which would cause a denial of service) and isolating the affected system (not shutting down an entire AI development platform or powering down an entire DMZ segment) are both explicitly preferred over indiscriminate shutdown; restoring affected systems from backup before containment is explicitly rejected (source, ransomware scenario: restoring could reinfect the restored systems and 'would destroy evidence needed to investigate the incident'); preserving forensic evidence is explicitly identified as 'the MOST important incident containment method consideration' (source, verbatim reasoning: if evidence is lost or damaged, 'the downstream incident response will be inconclusive'); turning off/powering down an affected system during active data exfiltration is explicitly rejected because it 'will result in a state change, which may result in the loss of forensic evidence' - blocking the malicious traffic is preferred; source explicitly frames containment and evidence preservation as being in tension ('there is a delicate balance between protecting evidence from an incident and containing an incident to prevent further impact'). No pattern invented: reuses the existing CANONICAL Pattern P01 (Business Alignment, already approved for Domain 4) for the scope-proportionality reasoning (a broad shutdown is not what the business actually needs) and Pattern P04 (No Lifecycle Jumping, already approved for Domain 4) for the containment-precedes-eradication/root-cause sequencing. Builds on concept.d4.escalation-communications (D4-U4): the same classified, escalated incident now requires a containment decision. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

display_name: Evidence and investigation: reliable understanding, disciplined handling
plain: Once an incident is contained, the organization still needs a reliable understanding of what actually happened - and that understanding depends on evidence handled with discipline, not collected or preserved hastily. The primary reason to maintain a chain of custody - a documented, unbroken record of who controlled the evidence and when - is to keep that evidence admissible and credible for legal, regulatory, disciplinary, or management decisions; a broken chain of custody, not physical damage to the evidence itself, is the bigger risk, because it undermines whether the evidence can be trusted at all. Investigation works from copies, not originals: forensic analysis performed on the original media risks contaminating it, so a verified image or copy is examined instead, preserving the original untouched. The information security manager coordinates the investigation and safeguards its integrity - recognizing when specialized forensic expertise is genuinely needed and bringing it in - without necessarily performing the forensic analysis personally. Investigation and containment pursue different immediate goals and can compete for attention: restoring systems and normal service too quickly, before evidence is preserved, can destroy exactly what the organization needs to understand the incident or support a later legal, regulatory, or disciplinary decision - in situations where the incident may lead to criminal charges, preventing contamination of evidence can take priority over how quickly service is restored. Deciding whether to involve law enforcement is a business decision that belongs to senior management, not something the investigator or the incident response team decides unilaterally; a third party performing forensic work does not transfer the organization's own accountability for how the investigation is handled.
